table.text: Next, we used polygenic scores (PGS) to further investigate genetic overlaps between dyslexia and socialinteraction outcomes. Because the heritability estimates for the social-based traits and their genetic correlations with dyslexia were low to modest (Suppl. Figure 1 and Suppl. (2017) (26) (see Methods for more details), the dyslexia GWAS summary statistics combined with the Lifelines sample sizes had >80% power to identify association representing genetic correlations of rg>0.02 (Suppl. Figure 2). PGS based on the GWAS summary statistics for loneliness, sociability, and social isolation each had 80% power to predict variance in dyslexia representative of rg>0.03, and subjective well-being had 80% power to identify an association representing a genetic correlation of rg>0.06 (Suppl. Figure 3A). Only the PGS for social trust had insufficient power to explain enough variation in dyslexia and was therefore excluded from the PGS analyses.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Dyslexia is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in reading and spelling.
Although social and emotional challenges have been reported in individuals with dyslexia, the genetic relationships between dyslexia, social functioning, and well-being remain poorly understood.
We combined phenotypic and genetic data from the Lifelines cohort with publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics.

Associations between dyslexia and social traits were examined using a multi-layered approach encompassing complementary methods, including phenotypic correlation analyses, polygenic score (PGS) analyses, linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC), and bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR).

Correlation analyses revealed significant phenotypic and genetic correlations between dyslexia and several social traits, including lower levels of life satisfaction, higher levels of loneliness, and less collegial support on the work floor.

PGS analyses demonstrated that genetic liability to dyslexia predicted lower life satisfaction and reduced support from colleagues in the workplace, whereas none of the social-based PGSs predicted dyslexia.

Bidirectional MR analyses provided evidence that genetic liability to dyslexia contributes to increased loneliness and social isolation, while no evidence was found for causal effects of social-interaction or well-being traits on dyslexia.
Together, our results consistently supported a directional relationship from dyslexia toward social and well-being outcomes.

In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that dyslexia shares genetic influences with social interaction and well-being traits and suggest that genetic liability for dyslexia contributes to adverse (psycho)social outcomes.

These results extend the impact of dyslexia beyond literacy-related difficulties and highlight the importance of providing social and structural support to individuals with dyslexia throughout the lifespan.
In modern human society, written communication is used on a daily basis to facilitate social interaction.

It serves multiple functions, including the transmission of information, expression of ideas, management of social relationships, articulation of needs, and transmission of knowledge and culture from one generation to the next.

In essence, writing refers to the ability to encode linguistic structures into written symbols with orthographic rules, while reading refers to the ability to decode these symbols to reconstruct meaning.
The level of skill for these complex processes differs among individuals, with more notable difficulties observed in individuals diagnosed with dyslexia (1).

text.text: Dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in accurate and/or fluent word reading and spelling, despite adequate intelligence and educational opportunities (2).
text.formatted: Dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in accurate and/or fluent word reading and spelling, despite adequate intelligence and educational opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: As reading and writing are fundamental skills for academic achievement and everyday functioning, understanding the nature and consequences of dyslexia is important.
Although written communication does not directly affect an individual's verbal ability in social interaction, evidence suggests an indirect relationship between literacy skills and social well-being.
For example, parents reported lower psychosocial functioning of their dyslexic children compared to typical readers already at 4 and 6 years of age, prior to their dyslexia diagnosis at age 8(3).
Problems with psychosocial functioning and social interactions continue after entering school (3, 4), as poor readers in the 3 rd grade are more likely to experience loneliness in the 5 th grade (5).

text.text: In adulthood, reading ability among typically developing readers correlates positively with social-emotional skills (r=0.23; 95%CI=0.19, 0.28) (6).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that individuals who experience difficulties with written communication may be at increased risk of challenges in social interaction across the lifespan.
The level of difficulties and prevalence of dyslexia diagnoses is higher within families, which is explained in part by a hereditary component as well as the influence of shared environment.
Reading outcomes are influenced by genetic components (7).

text.text: However, an upbringing in which a child is frequently encouraged to engage in reading activities also improves overall reading ability (8).

text.text: Genetic contributions to reading outcomes were first demonstrated in twin studies, where the heritability of a trait is deduced by using the difference in genetic similarity between mono-and dizygotic twins, while taking the shared environment to be constant.

The largest twin-based meta-analysis on reading ability to date estimated heritability for general reading (h 2 twin=66%), letter-word knowledge (h 2 twin=62%), phonological decoding (h 2 twin=68%), reading comprehension (h 2 twin=68%), phonological awareness (h 2 twin=52%), and spelling (h 2 twin=80%) (9).

text.text: Large-scale genotyping efforts enable researchers to quantify relatedness among unrelated individuals from their genetic information, giving opportunities to estimate heritability of complex traits using singlenucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data.

The regression of SNP data with phenotypic scores forms the basis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (10) that are used to identify DNA variants involved in heritable traits, and this approach has been applied to various reading-related traits. Doust et al. (2022) performed a GWAS on self-reported dyslexia, which was conducted in data of the direct-to-consumer genotyping company 23andMe (n=1,138,870 with ncases=51,800), and identified 42 significantly associated loci, with an estimated SNP-based heritability (h 2 SNP) of 0.18 (SE=0.008) (11). Eising et al. (2022) targeted five reading-and language-related skills in up to 34,000 people within the GenLang consortium and identified heritability for word reading (h 2 SNP=0.19; SE=0.021), nonword reading (h 2 SNP=0.26; SE=0.028), spelling (h 2 SNP=0.23; SE=0.031), phoneme awareness (h 2 SNP=0.25; SE=0.040), and nonword repetition(h 2 SNP=0.13; SE=0.039) (12).

text.text: The efforts of these large-scale GWAS studies have provided valuable data for further investigation of genetic associations with related outcomes, such as social interaction and well-being.
Few studies have investigated the shared genetic architecture between reading ability and social interaction experiences.

Indications of genetic overlap have been provided by Doust et al. (2022), as analyses of their GWAS summary statistics yielded a significant genetic correlation between dyslexia and loneliness (rg=0.24)(11), while Eising et al. (2022) found a positive correlation between the combined reading-traits that they studied and friendship satisfaction (rg=0.15; SE=0.058), as well as a negative relationship with loneliness (rg=-0.24; SE=0.048) (12).

text.text: However, genetic correlations between reading ability and a broader set of social interactive traits have not yet been investigated, nor has the power of genetic influences on reading ability as predictors of social outcomes.
Here, we investigated the shared genetic architecture and predictive power of dyslexia with respect to a range of social interactive traits.

We used published GWAS summary statistics of dyslexia (11) and several social-interaction traits(13-16) combined with quantitative trait and self-report data of similar traits and SNP data in the Lifelines(17) cohort; a multi-disciplinary prospective population-based cohort study of individuals living in the North of the Netherlands.

text.text: With these data, we i) assessed the relations between social-interactive traits in the Lifelines cohort using psychological network analysis, ii) investigated the shared genetic architecture between dyslexia and publicly available GWAS summary statistics representative of social interaction and well-being, iii) used polygenic score analysis to investigate the predictive power of genetic disposition to dyslexia for social-interactive outcomes and vice versa, and iv) 83 tested both directions of causality for SNPs robustly associated with dyslexia and social interactive 84 outcomes using two-sample mendelian randomization analysis.
Together, these findings provide a 85 comprehensive overview of the relationship between genetic architectures underlying dyslexia and social 86 well-being.

These findings show that i) there are indications that dyslexia-associated SNPs may be causal for loneliness and social isolation, and ii) the SNPs associated with sociability, social isolation, loneliness, subjective well-being, and social trust are not causal for dyslexia.

We investigated the phenotypic and genetic relations between dyslexia and social interaction/well-being traits using published GWAS summary statistics and direct phenotype and genotype data from the Lifelines cohort.
When considered collectively, the phenotypic correlations, PGS, genetic correlations, and MR results provided a nuanced picture of the relationship between dyslexia and social functioning.
First, we identified low yet significant phenotypic correlations between three reading traits and 13 measures of social interaction difficulties in adults.
With 87 out of 91 phenotypic correlations surviving Bonferroni correction (pBonferroni=0.05/91 tests=5.50E-4), we considered our phenotypic results robust.

Previous studies have reported social interaction difficulties in children with dyslexia prior to entering school(3), as well as during the schooling period(5,6), yet our results show that also adults with dyslexia experience more challenges in their daily social interaction.
Next, we examined genetic correlations between dyslexia and social traits, observing significant positive correlations with loneliness and social isolation.

Previous studies reported similar findings, with genetic correlations between dyslexia and loneliness (rg=0.24; SE=0.034) (11) and between reading ability and friendship satisfaction (rg=0.15; SE=0.058) and loneliness (rg=-0.24; SE=0.048)(12).

text.text: Higher PGS for dyslexia predicted overall lower life satisfaction and less support received from colleagues, whereas none of the social-trait PGSs predicted dyslexia.
Notably, the strongest PGS association of dyslexia was observed for workplace support from colleagues.

These work environment-specific experiences for individuals with dyslexia have been reported before, as they experience more challenges in work confidence (30) and social relationships with co-workers (31).

text.text: Lastly, MR analyses showed the same directional pattern, with evidence for dyslexia-related variants affecting loneliness and social isolation but no evidence that the social-based SNP-variants have causal effects on dyslexia.
Across PGS and MR analyses, our results suggested a directional relationship in which genetic disposition to dyslexia influences social outcomes rather than the reverse.
Evidence for this directionality was strongest for loneliness and social isolation.
Other studies also found correlations between dyslexia and heightened levels of self-perceived anxiety, depressive symptoms, and lower self-esteem (32) (33) (34).

text.text: The International Dyslexia Association(35) describe how reading difficulties in day-to-day life, in spite of continuous efforts to prevent writing and reading mistakes, can give a heightened sense of anxiety and frustration.

Furthermore, comparisons with typical readers in school, who can easily resolve reading and writing mistakes with practice, can lead to less confidence and lower levels of emotional well-being in individuals with dyslexia, with effects throughout the lifespan during schooling, studies, and working life.
This description fits with our findings, and would explain why the underlying genetics for dyslexia may be causal towards social-interactive and well-being outcomes, and not the other way around.
To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive investigation to date into the shared genetics underlying dyslexia and social well-being.

A study with a comparable PGS framework and focus examined developmental language disorder (DLD) in relation to common psychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, and ADHD (36).

text.text: That study found that individuals with DLD showed a stronger association between the genetic disposition for psychiatric disorders and conduct problems than individuals without DLD.
Given the high comorbidity between DLD and dyslexia (37), and the substantial genetic contribution to DLD (38), some overlap in social and behavioural outcomes may be expected.

text.text: Although direct comparisons of results for DLD and dyslexia across these studies cannot be made, these findings provide broader support that genetic liability for neurodevelopmental languagerelevant conditions may contribute to psychosocial outcomes later in life.

The strongest PGS association for dyslexia was observed for the amount of help received from colleagues on the work floor, where a higher genetic disposition for dyslexia predicted lower levels of perceived support (β=-0.48; p=0.007).

Importantly, this measure specifically reflects experiences within the workplace rather than broader social interactions, highlighting the work environment as a potentially important context in which dyslexia-related social challenges arise.
Previous studies examining dyslexia in the workplace relied primarily on phenotypic data and consistently reported difficulties and challenges.
For example, dyslexia severity has been associated with lower work confidence (r=-0.30, p<0.01) and stronger negative emotions unique to dyslexia (r = 0.37, p<0.01) (30).

text.text: In addition, a large meta-analysis that focussed on workplace experiences of individuals with dyslexia identified the largest effects for factors related to obtaining and maintaining employment, support from colleagues, and personal coping strategies (31).

text.text: A survey among employees with dyslexia suggested that employees with dyslexia particularly value workplace cultures characterized by awareness, inclusivity, and organizational support, highlighting the potential importance of supportive workplace environments for dyslexia-related challenges 48 .
Our results might suggest that these wishes are currently not fully met.

Given the central role of the workplace in adult life, these experiences may contribute to broader differences in well-being and life satisfaction, although this relationship was not evaluated in the present study.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the available GWAS summary statistics did not fully align with the available phenotypes in the Lifelines data.

For example, no comparable GWAS was available for workplace social support or social self-efficacy, disabling the evaluation of the associations between dyslexia and these social traits with LDSC and MR, and also disabling investigation of relationships of PGS for these social traits with dyslexia outcomes.

Second, although a range of sensitivity methods were applied, we cannot rule out violations of the MR assumptions or limited statistical power, particularly for the subjective well-being GWAS, for which only 8 SNPs met the 1E-6 significance threshold.

However, decent instrument strength was supported by the F-statistics exceeding the conventional threshold (F > 10), and also the secondary MR analyses using a larger number of suggestive genetic instruments (p<1E-6) did not provide evidence for causality.
text.formatted: However, decent instrument strength was supported by the F-statistics exceeding the conventional threshold (F > 10), and also the secondary MR analyses using a larger number of suggestive genetic instruments (p<1E-6) did not provide evidence for causality.

text.text: Third, the PGSs used in this study only captured a proportion of the underlying genetic liability in the Lifelines cohort.

For example, the PGSdyslexia only explained 5.6% of the variance for dyslexia in the Lifelines cohort, while the captured h 2 SNP in both the Lifelines (h 2 snp = 13%) and the 23andMe sample (h 2 SNP = 16%) was higher.

Consequently, the PGS analyses with dyslexia and social traits captures only the component of genetic liability represented by the available genetic instruments and may therefore not fully reflect the genetic architecture underlying and relationships between these traits.
Fourth, both dyslexia diagnoses and social-interactive measures were based on self-report, which might be less reliable compared to a clinical derived diagnoses or scores derived by an assessment.
The prevalence for self-reported dyslexia diagnoses in the 23andMe sample (5%) (11) was slightly lower compared to the prevalence in the typical United States population (5.3-11.8%) (41).

text.text: The social-based measures in the Lifelines data were self-reported as well, though all scores were derived from validated instruments, and were therefore considered as reliable and robust.
Lastly, this study lacks ancestral diversity, as all analysis were conducted in individuals from European ancestry, which limits the generalizability of our findings to other populations (43).

text.text: Follow-up studies should investigate whether these findings replicate in samples of non-European ancestry.

This study provides empirical evidence that genetic disposition to dyslexia is associated with social interaction and well-being outcomes, while also offering insight into the potential directional relationship between dyslexia and overall well-being and life satisfaction.

Together, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of the impact of dyslexia beyond literacy-related difficulties, highlighting its relevance for social and psychosocial functioning across the lifespan.

We hope that this work encourages greater recognition of the challenges experienced by individuals with dyslexia and supports the development of targeted interventions and structural support systems that promote well-being and social participation throughout all stages of life.

text.text: The network consists of nodes representing observed variables, which are connected by edges representing statistical relationships.
Estimation of the model is done using the Markov random field approach, where edges represent a full conditional association between two nodes after conditioning on all other nodes in the network.
The resulting edges are defined as partial correlation coefficients.

Mixed graphical models (21, 22) are an extension of the Gaussian-Ising model and the class of exponential family Markov Random Fields, which allows for modelling of traits following binomial, continuous and categorical distributions within one network.

text.text: Furthermore, it allows for correlations within and between different groups of variables and the model does not enforce connections across all nodes if a statistical relationship is absent.

Cleaned genotype data (filtering steps included INFO > 0.8, MAF>0.01, HWE p≤10 -6 , and call-rate>0.99) from 36,339 individuals and 548,029 markers were imputed with the Sanger imputation service using the Haplotype Reference Consortium reference panel (version r1.1), resulting in a total of 7,424,407 imputed SNPs.

text.text: The second sample (UGLI2, release 2) was genotyped on the FinnGen Thermo Fisher Axiom custom array.

The cleaned genotype data (the same filtering criteria used for UGLI1 were applied) of a total of 28,149 participants and 460,136 markers were imputed following the same protocol as used for UGLI1, resulting in a total of 7,474,700 imputed SNPs.
For follow-up analyses, we used the principal components (PCs) provided by Lifelines, with PC scores generated separately for the genotyped individuals in UGLI1 and UGLI2.
Further details about the genetic data provided by Lifelines can be found on their online wiki-page (https://wiki-lifelines.web.rug.nl/doku.php?id=ugli).

text.text: Filtering and merging were done with PLINK (v1.90b6.10).
SNP-based heritability (h 2 SNP) was estimated using genome-wide complex trait analysis-genomic restricted maximum likelihood (GCTA-GREML) software(18) (version 1.93.2).
The h 2 SNP represents the proportion of phenotypic variance explained by the variation in genetic relatedness, captured by a genetic relationship matrix (GRM) estimated from genotyped SNPs.
The genetic correlation represents the proportion of genetic variance that is shared between two traits, based on the GRM estimates.
Analyses were performed using the threshold-GRM approach(52) which allows related and unrelated individuals to be analysed jointly.

A second GRM was constructed by setting relationship coefficient values (π) of <0.02 to 0, which enables simultaneous estimation of the pedigree heritability (h 2 pedigree) and heritability explained by genotyped SNPs (h 2 SNP).
text.formatted: A second GRM was constructed by setting relationship coefficient values (π) of <0.02 to 0, which enables simultaneous estimation of the pedigree heritability (h 2 pedigree) and heritability explained by genotyped SNPs (h 2 SNP).

text.text: Modelling both GRMs together with GREML helps to distinguish SNP-associated genetic effects from additional familial resemblance, thereby reducing upward bias in SNP-heritability estimates due to shared environmental and pedigree-associated effects.
Gender, genotype batch, age at time of assessment and the first 10 PCs were included as covariates.
Publicly available GWAS summary statistics representative of reading and social-interaction were selected for this study.
We used the dyslexia GWAS summary statistics as the reading-based measure, which was based on self-report diagnoses of dyslexia ("Have you been diagnosed with dyslexia?"

text.text: We also selected five sets of social-interaction and well-being based GWAS summary statistics.
The subjective well-being GWAS summary statistics came from a meta-analysis study of items evaluating levels of happiness (16).
text.formatted: The subjective well-being GWAS summary statistics came from a meta-analysis study of items evaluating levels of happiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: The original meta-analysis consisted of 59 participating cohorts with a total sample size of n=298,420.
However, the publicly available data from that well-being study do not contain the 23andMe cohort.
Furthermore, as the GWAS metaanalysis also included the Lifelines cohort, we received GWAS results excluding Lifelines.
The final total sample size included 192,994 individuals.

All three loneliness-based measures (sociability, loneliness, and social isolation) were constructed from composite-scores in UK Biobank: the sociability GWAS summary statistic was based on (1) frequency of family/friends visits, (2) number and type of visited social venues, (3) worrying about social embarrassment, and (4) loneliness experience, with 342,461 participating individuals(14).

The loneliness GWAS summary statistics were constructed from (1) frequency of feeling lonely, (2) number of individuals in the household, (3) frequency of family/friends visits, and (4) the ability to confide in someone, with a total of 452,302 individuals(13).

GWAS summary statistics for social isolation were derived from (1) frequency of family/friends visits, (2) ability to confide in someone, and (3) number of social activities per week, with a sample size of 449,609(15) individuals.

Lastly, the social trust GWAS summary statistics were based on a composite score of (1) trustworthiness of other people, (2) if others take advantage of you, and (3) if others display altruistic behaviour (25).

text.text: LDSC software (v1.0.1) was used to munge summary statistics, followed by estimation of the heritability and genetic correlations.
LD scores were based on the phase 3 1000 Genomes Project European reference genome panel, and analyses were restricted to a predefined set of HapMap 3 SNPs.
Power calculations were performed in order to estimate the expected predictive accuracy of PGS derived from selected GWAS summary statistics in Lifelines.

First, the maximum possible prediction accuracy R² for the summary statistic was estimated by fitting the variant effect sizes using a best linear unbiased prediction(26), where h 2 corresponds to the summary statistic-based h 2 SNP as estimated with LDSC, N represents the GWAS sample size, and M represents the number of independent common variants that inform the PGS (for these analyses, M was based on the number of independent common SNPs that are present on a standard genotyping array for European ancestry (53), which is M = 60,000).
text.formatted: First, the maximum possible prediction accuracy R² for the summary statistic was estimated by fitting the variant effect sizes using a best linear unbiased prediction(26), where h 2 corresponds to the summary statistic-based h 2 SNP as estimated with LDSC, N represents the GWAS sample size, and M represents the number of independent common variants that inform the PGS (for these analyses, M was based on the number of independent common SNPs that are present on a standard genotyping array for European ancestry <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(53)</ref>, which is M = 60,000).

text.text: The maximum possible R² value for a within-trait predictor-outcome trait combination (e.g. dyslexiadyslexia) was used to further inform R² for cross-trait predictor-outcome trait combinations (e.g. dyslexialife satisfaction).

We multiplied the maximum R² of the predictor GWAS with the genetic correlation (rg) between dyslexia and social traits, as estimated with LDSC, to account for the level of shared genetic variance in the cross-trait PGS analysis.
Then, we used a range of R² values to estimate the power for the cross-trait PGS analyses using simulations.

First, a multivariate normal distribution was generated with mean 0 and a correlation parameter r defined as the square root of the adjusted R² , with the sample size equal to that of the outcome trait.
Subsequently, a regression was conducted across the constructed multivariate data.
Simulations were repeated 10,000 times, where the power was estimated based on the frequency (percentage) of successful predictions (where p<0.0125).
text.formatted: Simulations were repeated 10,000 times, where the power was estimated based on the frequency (percentage) of successful predictions (where p<0.0125).

text.text: Regression analyses were conducted in R (v4.2.2) using the glm() function for binary outcomes, and the lm() function for continuous outcomes.

First, the null model was constructed with the age at the time of assessment, the first five PC's, and gender as predictors, and the z-standardized phenotype score for dyslexia or social-based trait as outcome.
The PGS-model included the z-standardized PGS as predictor as well.
For the regressions with a binary outcome, McFadden R² values were calculated based on the fitted model's log likelihood values, and odds ratios were derived from the regression results.
For the regressions with a continuous outcome, incremental R² values were estimated by deducting the nullmodel r 2 from the PGS-model r 2 , and β-estimates were derived from the PGS-model.

The causal effect of exposure-associated SNPs on the outcome was estimated using the Mendelian Randomization (MR) framework, which uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to study the causal effect of an exposure (the instrumental SNPs associated with the exposure trait) on an outcome.
Within the MR framework, three core assumptions must be met for the results to provide reliable evidence of causality (55, 56).
text.formatted: Within the MR framework, three core assumptions must be met for the results to provide reliable evidence of causality <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56)</ref>.

text.text: First, the instrumental variants must be robustly associated with the exposure.
Therefore, only SNPs reaching genome-wide significance (p <5E-8) in the exposure GWAS were selected as instruments.
text.formatted: Therefore, only SNPs reaching genome-wide significance (p <5E-8) in the exposure GWAS were selected as instruments.

text.text: Second, the instrumental variants must be independent of potential confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship.
Third, the instrumental variants must not directly affect the outcome, MR analyses were conducted using the TwoSampleMR(28,29) (v0.6.11) package in R (v4.2.1).
Instrument strength towards the exposure was assessed with the F-statistic(58), retaining only those with F>10 to reduce bias from weak instruments.
text.formatted: Instrument strength towards the exposure was assessed with the F-statistic(58), retaining only those with F>10 to reduce bias from weak instruments.

text.text: Next, causal effects were inferred from the SNP-exposure and SNPoutcome associations combined.

The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method was used as the primary method, as recommended by the MR guidelines (55), which combines SNP-specific Wald ratios and provides an unbiased estimate when all instrumental variable assumptions are met or when pleiotropy is balanced.
text.formatted: The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method was used as the primary method, as recommended by the MR guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55)</ref>, which combines SNP-specific Wald ratios and provides an unbiased estimate when all instrumental variable assumptions are met or when pleiotropy is balanced.

text.text: Additional sensitivity analyses were performed to assess robustness of the results and potential MR violations.

These included the MR Egger regression, which allows for directional pleiotropy by estimating an intercept term, the Weighted median estimator, which provides a consistent estimate if at least 50% of the weight comes from valid instruments, and the Weighted mode and Simple mode, which identify the most common causal effect estimate across SNPs under different clustering assumptions.

Follow-up sensitivity analyses for heterogeneity and pleiotropy were further evaluated using regression diagnostics and graphical inspection of SNP-specific effects, including funnel and scatter plots.

Influence analyses were performed using leave-one-out analyses to assess whether results were driven by individual SNPs, and SNP-specific Wald ratio estimates were examined in relation to their standard errors to identify potential outliers.
